title: Grünfeld Defence, Exchange Variation: attack the big centre
outcomes: Names the pawn centre after 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.e4 Nxc3 6.bxc3 (pawns on c3, d4, e4) and finds Black's ...c5 break against d4
Keeps d4 defended and develops a piece instead of capturing on c5 with the d-pawn
Checks which white pieces defend a2 before the queen takes it, and sees that a rook on a1 or a queen on d2 decides it
Recognises a Grünfeld position where White has no e4 pawn, and checks before playing ...c5 instead of assuming the break works.

steps.text: **Grünfeld Defence** (ECO D80): 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 d5. Black leaves White the centre, then attacks it with pieces and the ...c5 break. In our online sample (4,752,291 games, September 2026) 5,371 visits reach this position; 2,375 continue 4.cxd5 Nxd5, the Exchange Variation (D85). This lesson follows that line and each side's plan. Centre control and pawn breaks are not re-taught here.

steps.caption: Position after 3...d5, White to move. Step through one main line of the Exchange Variation. Other moves exist; this line shows the structure and where each plan starts.

line.say: White takes the pawn: the Exchange Variation begins.
e4 attacks the knight and builds a big pawn centre.
The knight takes on c3, removing the attacker.
bxc3 recaptures: White now has pawns on c3, d4 and e4.
The bishop on g7 aims along the diagonal at d4.
The break: the pawn on c5 attacks d4.
Be3 develops and defends d4 again.
The queen attacks the pawn on c3.
Qd2 defends c3 and the pawn on a2.
Rc1 develops the rook and defends c3.

claims.statement: After ...Nxc3 a black knight stands on c3.
After e4 the pawn attacks the knight on d5.
After bxc3 a white pawn stands on c3.
The white pawn still stands on d4.
The white pawn still stands on e4.
After Nf3 the knight defends d4.
After Be3 the bishop defends d4.
After Qd2 the queen defends c3 and a2.
After O-O the black king is on g8.
After Rc1 the rook defends c3.

steps.text: **Black's plan: the c5 break (rule of thumb).** Black lets White hold d4 and e4, then attacks d4 with the pawn on c5, the bishop on g7 and later the queen. Condition: a white pawn stands on d4 to be attacked. Masters (329,379 games, both players 2,500 or more): after 7.Nf3, Black played ...c5 in 1,151 of 1,192 games. Find the break.

**What strong players chose.** Masters, after 6...Bg7 (1,944 games): 7.Nf3 861, 7.Bc4 483, 7.Be3 303, 7.Qa4+ 208, 7.Bb5+ 70. After 7.Nf3 c5 8.Be3, Black played ...Qa5 in 373 of 507. These count games; they are not evaluations.
**White's plan (rule of thumb):** keep d4 and e4 defended, develop the pieces, and do not trade the centre away. Next: the tempting capture.

**Check before taking (rule of thumb).** Before the queen takes a2, ask which white pieces defend a2. If one does, the capture loses the queen for a pawn; if none does, it is at least not an immediate loss, which does not make it good. In one position below White has no pawn on e4, and the engine rates an immediate ...c5 at least 0.4 pawn worse (its reason was not checked). Predict the next three.

steps.title: One piece changes whether the queen can take a2
steps.prompt: Three positions with the black queen attacked by the bishop on d2. The second differs from the first only in White's rook (a1 instead of b1). The third differs from the first only in Black's h-pawn (h6 instead of h7). Predict, then check.
Think about the positions you played without hints. Before you chose a move, what did you check? Write one line for each side.
